article.audioclf.title: Fine-tuning DistilHuBERT for music genre classification
article.audioclf.subtitle: Audio deep learning project based on the GTZAN dataset: audio signal preprocessing, adaptation of a pretrained transformer and performance analysis on a music classification task.
article.audioclf.overview.title: Overview
article.audioclf.overview.text: The goal was to automatically classify music excerpts according to their genre, starting directly from raw audio signals. The project shows how to prepare waveforms, convert them into the format expected by DistilHuBERT, and fine-tune the model to recognize 10 different music genres.
article.audioclf.dataset.title: Dataset
article.audioclf.dataset.text: The project uses GTZAN, a classic music classification dataset composed of 1000 audio excerpts divided into 10 genres. Each sample corresponds to a 30-second music excerpt. Since the dataset is relatively balanced, a simple train/test split is enough to evaluate the model on unseen data.
article.audioclf.preprocessing.title: Audio preprocessing
article.audioclf.preprocessing.text: Audio excerpts are resampled to 16 kHz to match the input format expected by the pretrained model. Preprocessing is applied on the fly (meaning directly during the training loop) using the feature extractor: signals are truncated if necessary, normalized, then converted into tensors that can be processed by the transformer. This approach avoids storing precomputed features and keeps the pipeline lighter.
article.audioclf.model.title: Model
article.audioclf.model.text:
The model used here is DistilHuBERT, a distilled and lighter version of HuBERT, with around 23 million parameters. Unlike models that operate on spectrograms, DistilHuBERT directly takes a raw audio waveform as input after resampling and normalization.

I chose this model because it is more compact than larger audio transformers while still keeping strong audio representations learned from large-scale datasets. It is therefore a good compromise for a fine-tuning notebook: powerful enough to achieve good results, while remaining easier to train on Google Colab.

In practice, fine-tuning reuses the pretrained backbone, which already knows how to extract general audio representations, and replaces the original classification head with a new one adapted to the 10 GTZAN genres. Training then adjusts the model weights to specialize these representations on my music data instead of learning the whole audio structure from scratch.
article.audioclf.training.title: Training
article.audioclf.training.text: Training is performed using the Hugging Face Trainer API. The notebook defines the main hyperparameters: batch size, gradient accumulation, learning rate, scheduler, warmup, weight decay and evaluation at each epoch. After a first training phase, a second fine-tuning phase is launched with a different learning rate to improve validation accuracy.
article.audioclf.inference.title: Evaluation
article.audioclf.inference.text: After training, the model is evaluated on the test set. The analysis does not stop at global accuracy: a confusion matrix and a classification report help identify which genres are well separated and which ones remain harder to distinguish.
article.audioclf.results.title: Results
article.audioclf.results.text: The notebook reaches a test accuracy of around 87%, which is a strong result on GTZAN for such a compact model. Most genres are correctly recognized. The main confusions occur between rock, metal and country, which is not very surprising since these genres share many instrumental characteristics such as guitar, bass and drums. In this case, the confusion matrix helps relate the model errors to actual musical similarities.
article.audioclf.conclusion.title: Conclusion and future work
article.audioclf.conclusion.text:
This project allowed me to build a complete audio classification pipeline using a pretrained transformer model. Fine-tuning DistilHuBERT makes it possible to obtain strong performances without training a model from scratch, by adapting general audio representations to a specific music classification task.

The results are very encouraging, with an accuracy close to 87%. The remaining errors mostly come from musically similar genres, which shows that the limitation does not only come from the model itself but also from the nature of the classes. Future improvements could include testing other audio backbones, evaluating the model on multiple splits, or building a small inference interface to test the classifier on new songs.
